claims.evidence: BHF ECG page: Holter/ambulatory ECG is continuous recording over 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer; useful because palpitations do not occur constantly.
NTH leaflet: loop recorder constantly monitors, unlike an ECG or 24 hour monitor, and can stay in place for up to three years.
BHF ECG page: continuous recording over about 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer.
BHF ECG page: helps with atrial fibrillation or the cause of palpitations that do not happen all the time.
BHF: recorder is returned to the hospital when the test finishes; hospital Holter leaflets give a symptom diary to log symptoms.
NTH leaflet: loop recorder under the skin of the chest, constant monitoring unlike ECG/24 hour monitor, in place for up to three years.
A resting ECG capturing only seconds was not stated in retrieved text; plain textbook fact.
BHF ECG page describes Holter/ambulatory ECG as continuous recording over about 24 to 48 hours, sometimes longer.
BHF ECG page: helps find atrial fibrillation or cause of palpitations that do not happen constantly.
BHF: electrodes on the chest, small recorder worn on a belt at the waist, wires taped down.
BHF: normal activities except bath or shower. Swimming not stated by BHF; some leaflets give spare electrodes for showering on longer wear, so a blanket 'not possible' is too strong.
claims.newSentence: The person can carry on with most normal activities, but the monitor must be kept dry, so leaflets say not to bath or shower while it is worn.

claims.evidence: Hospital Holter leaflets/diary page: diary records time, activity and symptoms such as palpitations or dizziness.
BHF: when the test is finished you return the recorder to the hospital.
Event recorder leaflet: a button is pressed if you have symptoms; but the device can also record automatically, so 'only when symptoms happen' is too strong.
claims.newSentence: Some monitors, such as an event recorder, have a button the wearer presses when they have symptoms.

claims.evidence: R test event recorder is worn for five to seven days.
NTH: loop recorder constantly monitors unlike an ECG or 24 hour monitor. 'Where shorter tests have not explained symptoms' was not explicitly retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A hospital leaflet describes an implantable loop recorder, which monitors the heart constantly, unlike an ECG or 24-hour monitor.

claims.evidence: NHS leaflets: placed just under the skin on the front of the chest, usually the left side, under local anaesthetic; records automatically anything outside normal and when the activator is pressed.
ULH leaflet: device does not deliver shocks or other therapy, only records rhythm; up to three years per NHS leaflets (Royal Papworth gives a longer range, battery varies by model).
NHS leaflets: activator pressed when symptoms occur; device stores rhythm from before activation.
ULH: data sent wirelessly to the healthcare team via home transmitter or smartphone app. Leaflets say it is not a 24/7 monitoring service; 'person is contacted' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Data is often sent to the healthcare team wirelessly through a home transmitter or smartphone app.

claims.evidence: BHF: the test is safe and completely painless, though some electrodes are very sticky.
Barts/ULH leaflets: the implantable loop recorder acts as a monitor and does not deliver therapy. Not shown for BHF page or Holter.
claims.newSentence: An implantable loop recorder only monitors and records; it does not deliver shocks or other treatment.

claims.evidence: NHS palpitations page: call 999 if palpitations persist with chest pain, shortness of breath, or feeling faint or fainting; see a GP if they keep coming back or are worrying. NHS 111 for palpitations was not confirmed; 'severe' breathlessness not stated.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises calling 999 if palpitations come with chest pain, shortness of breath or feeling faint, and seeing a GP if they keep coming back or are worrying.

notes: WebSearch summaries blend pages; urls given where title/excerpt matched. Wearable event-recorder facts come from NHS trust pages not in author list. c07 is the single textbook item. Swimming on Holter not confirmed.
